newsitem.title: UK: Romania inflation target still ambitious-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Romania inflation target still ambitious-analysts.

text.p: Romania's new year-on-year inflation estimate of 110 percent for this year, up from a previous forecast of 89.5 percent, was still ambitious, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It's still an ambitious target...I think it would be near 150 percent," ING Barings economist Parvoleta Shtereva told Reuters.

On Tuesday, Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, who heads the new centrist-coalition government, revised up the year-on-year inflation estimate for 1997 but said it would be no more than 110 percent.

In a state-of-the-nation address marking almost 200 days since his cabinet took office after ousting ex-communists, Ciorbea also forecast a slowdown in monthly inflation in coming months, in line with promises under accords with international lenders.
The International Monetary Fund approved last month $430 million in credits for Romania, which pledged to cut monthly inflation to about 2.2 percent by end-1997.
Ciorbea estimated inflation at six percent in May and rates of two to three percent by the end of the year, ruling out inflationary shocks in the months ahead.
But analysts said on Wednesday Ciorbea's monthly estimates did not match his year-on-year forecast.
"Those numbers don't add up. If we consider (Ciorbea's) monthly forecasts we have a year-on-year range of 130 to 145 percent," said Merrill Lynch analyst Andrew Kenningham.

April's inflation was 6.9 percent, sharply down from a record high of 30.7 percent in March after the government moved to free fuel, energy and food prices. Consumer prices were 89 percent up in April from December 1996.
"It's quite clear price distortions were much bigger than expected," Shtereva said.
"There's nothing bad in that because it includes administrative price correction. They could have come up with a more realistic (year-on-year) figure."
Despite that ambitious year-on-year figure, analysts said, most important for the Balkan country was to bring inflation under control and achieve lower monthly rates.
"What counts is to get a slowdown in the second half of the year," said David Mars, emerging market director at SBC Warburg.

Romania pledged to implement radical reforms this year, including a tight budgetary policies, lower current account deficit as well as faster privatisation and restructuring of communist-era industries and farms.
Inflation was 56.9 percent in 1996, up from 27.8 percent the previous year but lower than rates of 61.7 and 300 percent in 1994 and 1993 respectively.
